chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
## The Pivot

In November 2024, FREYR Battery S.A. did something few investors in the Norwegian lithium-ion manufacturer had anticipated when it joined the New York Stock Exchange three years earlier: it bought a solar factory. The target was Trina Solar's 5-gigawatt module manufacturing facility in Wilmer, Texas — a 1.35 million square-foot plant that had begun producing panels just weeks before the transaction was signed. The acquisition price was $340 million in blended consideration: $100 million cash, a $50 million intercompany loan repayment, a $150 million loan note, and equity representing 9.9% of FREYR's outstanding common stock, with an $80 million convertible note exchangeable for a further 11.5% stake. The company also assumed $235 million of facility-related debt. [Solar Power World](https://www.solarpowerworldonline.com/2024/11/freyr-buys-trina-solar-panel-factory-in-texas-for-340-million/) It was, in its totality, a bet-the-company transaction — not on batteries, but on glass and silicon.

The deal closed in December 2024. By February 19, 2025, FREYR Battery had ceased to exist as a corporate identity. In its place: T1 Energy Inc. (NYSE: TE), headquartered in Austin, Texas, with Daniel Barcelo as Chairman and Chief Executive Officer. [BusinessWire](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20250219161823/en/FREYR-Battery-Rebrands-as-T1-Energy) The ticker changed from FREY to TE at the open of business on March 3, 2025. T1 Energy operates US solar module manufacturing at the Wilmer facility — rebranded G1 Dallas — alongside residual battery-cell development assets at Mo i Rana, Norway, that have been de-prioritised. The company's strategic posture is US solar module manufacturing under the Inflation Reduction Act's Section 45X advanced manufacturing production tax credit framework.

## From Fjord to Texas: The FREYR Heritage

The corporate lineage traces to 2018, when Norwegian entrepreneur Tom Einar Jensen co-founded FREYR Battery in Mo i Rana — a remote Arctic industrial town whose abundant hydroelectric grid was positioned as a structural advantage in Europe's emerging battery race. In January 2021, FREYR announced a business combination with Alussa Energy Acquisition Corp., the Houston-based SPAC, valuing the company at approximately $1.4 billion and offering up to $850 million in gross proceeds including a $600 million PIPE. The NYSE listing followed in July 2021 under the ticker FREY. [BusinessWire](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20210128006233/en/FREYR-a-Developer-of-Clean-Next-Generation-Battery-Cells-to-List-on-NYSE-Through-a-Business-Combination-with-Alussa-Energy-Acquisition-Corp.)

The promises ran into the reality of battery manufacturing economics. The Customer Qualification Plant at Mo i Rana advanced through construction in 2022–2023, but the broader industry confronted raw-material volatility, Chinese overcapacity pressure, and the evaporation of the SPAC-era valuation premium. A US gigafactory project in Atlanta was announced and subsequently scaled back. Daniel Barcelo, who succeeded Jensen as CEO during the 2023–2024 strategic reset, presided over the pivot that followed.

## G1 Dallas: First Year at Scale

The Wilmer facility inherited Trina Solar's full operational team at closing. Trina's Dave Gustafson joined T1 as Chief Operating Officer; Mingxing Lin, former head of Trina's overseas finance centre, joined as Chief Strategy Officer. Production scaling was rapid: G1 Dallas produced 443 megawatts in Q1 2025 — 96% of plan — and reached daily run rates above nameplate capacity before year-end. [T1 Energy IR](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-reports-first-quarter-2025-results) Full-year 2025 output was 2.79 gigawatts, with Q4 alone contributing 1.17 gigawatts. [PV-Tech](https://www.pv-tech.org/t1-energy-produced-2-8gw-solar-modules-in-2025-forecasts-up-to-4-2gw-in-2026/)

Net sales for full-year 2025 totalled $755.3 million, with a net loss of $380.8 million reflecting the capital structure inherited from both the battery era and the Trina debt assumption. [T1 Energy IR](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-results) Barcelo framed the result in the Q4 earnings release:

> "2025 was a defining year for T1 Energy as we advanced our strategy to build America's first vertically integrated, silicon-based solar platform. We expanded our commercial partnerships, highlighted by a long-term offtake agreement with Treaty Oak Clean Energy, ramped production and sales at our fully operational G1_Dallas facility, and secured over $440 million in strategic capital to accelerate our growth and enhance T1's competitive position as an American solar leader."

## Section 45X: The Policy Underpinning

Section 45X of the Inflation Reduction Act provides $0.07 per watt for US-manufactured solar modules, with additional credits for cells and wafers. At G1 Dallas's 5 gigawatt nameplate running at full scale, the implied annual credit value approaches $350 million. T1 accrued $92 million in Section 45X credits during 2025, then completed the company's first credit sale: a $160 million transaction executed at $0.91 per dollar of PTC to an investment-grade US financial institution. The company's eligibility for Section 45X survived initial Treasury guidance on Foreign Entity of Concern restrictions — a critical test given Trina Solar's Chinese parentage — with Treasury's preliminary FEOC framework described as consistent with T1's analysis. For 2026, G1 Dallas guided production of 3.1 to 4.2 gigawatts, contingent on demand and cell supply. [PV Magazine](https://pv-magazine-usa.com/2026/05/14/how-t1-energy-is-ramping-up-multi-gigawatt-u-s-solar-manufacturing/) Construction on Phase 1 of the planned G2 cell manufacturing facility in Austin had commenced within the snapshot window.

## The Central Tension

What T1 Energy accomplished in roughly eighteen months — pivoting from battery-cell ambitions in the Norwegian Arctic to a gigawatt-scale module factory in the Dallas exurbs — is uncommon in the history of NYSE clean-energy companies. The inherited FREYR CIK (0001992243) now anchors a filing history that runs from Mo i Rana construction reports to Texas production records. The dossier that follows asks the harder questions. How does G1 Dallas operational scaling proceed, and what does the wide 3.1-to-4.2-gigawatt 2026 guidance range signal about demand visibility? What does Section 45X deliver net of FEOC compliance costs, monetisation discounts, and the evolving IRA policy environment? How does T1 compete against First Solar — the only comparably scaled US pure-play module manufacturer, with deep utility-scale relationships and a more resolved balance sheet? And what is the residual strategic posture for the Norway battery assets, which remain on the books at de-prioritised status but have not been formally divested?

---

chapters.title: From 2018 FREYR Battery founding through SPAC, Atlanta reset, and Trina pivot
chapters.body:
The Norwegian battery manufacturer that listed on the New York Stock Exchange in the summer of 2021 with ambitions to challenge the global lithium-ion supply chain from an Arctic Norway industrial city had, by early 2025, renamed itself T1 Energy, relocated its headquarters to Austin, Texas, and staked its future on American solar module manufacturing under the shelter of the Inflation Reduction Act. The journey from FREYR Battery's founding to that repositioning compressed nearly every industrial-era corporate archetype — the visionary founding, the capital-markets moment, the strategic reset, the acquisition pivot — into less than seven years.

## Origins: The Nordic Battery Thesis, 2018–2020

Tom Einar Jensen founded FREYR Battery in 2018 with a thesis constructed around an accident of Norwegian geography. Mo i Rana, a small industrial city on Norway's northern coastline near the Arctic Circle, sat adjacent to abundant and structurally cheap hydroelectric power — electricity that could underpin a battery cell manufacturing cost structure meaningfully below what coal- or gas-heavy grids could support elsewhere in Europe. Jensen, an entrepreneur with roots in the Norwegian energy industry, saw in the global lithium-ion buildout a gap that clean-power Norway was uniquely positioned to fill.

The site-selection logic was compelling on paper. Norway's electricity grid runs approximately 90 percent renewable — predominantly hydro — and power prices at Mo i Rana reflected that abundance. For a lithium-ion cell manufacturing process that draws heavily on electricity for electrode processing, drying, and cell formation, the grid advantage translated directly into per-kilowatt-hour cell cost savings. Jensen framed FREYR as a European battery champion that could supply the continent's accelerating electric-vehicle transition and stationary storage demand without the carbon intensity of Asian supply chains — a narrative that carried both environmental credibility and supply-security appeal to European OEMs increasingly anxious about Chinese battery dependence.

The company attracted early institutional capital against that thesis and grew as a Norwegian private entity before the scale of ambition outpaced what domestic capital markets could readily absorb.

## SPAC to NYSE: The July 2021 Listing

The path to US public markets ran through the blank-check vehicle that defined the 2020–2021 capital markets era. FREYR Battery agreed to merge with Alussa Energy Acquisition Corp, a special purpose acquisition company, in a transaction that closed in July 2021. The deal implied a post-merger enterprise valuation of approximately $1.4 billion, placing FREYR among the larger European battery start-ups to access US equity markets at the apex of the SPAC cycle.

The timing was fortuitous from a capital-raising standpoint and treacherous from a benchmarking one. The post-SPAC prospectus laid out a sequenced buildout: a Customer Qualification Plant at Mo i Rana to validate the cell chemistry and production process, followed by a full-scale Norwegian gigafactory, followed by a US manufacturing footprint. It was an ambitious multi-act programme for a pre-revenue industrial company operating in one of the most capital-intensive sectors in the clean-energy transition.

| Era | Key Event | Date |
|---|---|---|
| Founding | FREYR Battery established, Mo i Rana thesis | 2018 |
| Public markets | SPAC merger with Alussa Energy; NYSE: FREY | July 2021 |
| Construction | Mo i Rana CQP active; Giga America announced | 2022–2023 |
| Reset | Jensen departs; Barcelo takes command; Giga America scaled back | 2023–2024 |
| Acquisition | Trina Solar Wilmer Texas 5 GW facility acquired | November 2024 |
| Rename | T1 Energy Inc.; NYSE: TE; Austin HQ | Q1 2025 |

## Building the CQP and the American Ambition, 2022–2023

The post-SPAC years were defined by construction in Norway and announcement in the United States. At Mo i Rana, the Customer Qualification Plant advanced from blueprint to operational infrastructure — a proving ground engineered not to produce commercial volume but to generate the production-process data and certified cell samples required by potential offtake customers before any gigafactory capital commitment. The CQP was a deliberate sequencing decision: qualify the chemistry, secure the customers, then scale.

In parallel, FREYR pivoted aggressively toward the United States following the passage of the Inflation Reduction Act in August 2022. The company announced what it branded Giga America, a proposed multi-gigawatt battery cell manufacturing facility in Georgia, targeting the Southeast's growing clean-energy industrial corridor and positioning FREYR to capture the domestic-content and advanced-manufacturing incentives embedded in the IRA. The dual-geography strategy — Norway for technology validation, the United States for scale — reflected both the geopolitics of the moment and the institutional appetite for US-domiciled clean-energy industrial assets.

The ambition of that two-continent buildout demanded capital that the battery industry was beginning to question.

## The Battery Reset: Jensen Departs, Barcelo Takes Command, 2023–2024

The strategic reset that arrived in 2023 was not unique to FREYR — it swept across the western battery start-up landscape with structural force. Chinese cell manufacturers, principally CATL and BYD, had continued scaling aggressively through the post-pandemic period, driving cell costs toward levels that subjected western greenfield capacity to severe economic pressure. EV demand growth in key markets softened from the rates embedded in the most aggressive capacity projections, easing the urgency of European and US original equipment manufacturers to pay a premium for secured non-Chinese supply.

Against that backdrop, Giga America was scaled back materially. The Georgia facility, positioned in 2022 as a flagship commitment, was reduced in near-term scope as management conducted a cost-base review and reassessed the capital allocation logic of a dual-continent battery manufacturing buildout for a company of FREYR's size and liquidity profile.

The leadership transition that accompanied the reset was decisive. Tom Einar Jensen stepped back from the chief executive role. Daniel Barcelo succeeded him, inheriting both the Mo i Rana asset and the fundamental strategic question of what FREYR's forward platform should look like. The Norway operations were not abandoned; the Mo i Rana CQP continued to operate and generate technical learning. But they receded in strategic priority as Barcelo assessed the options.

## The Trina Pivot: Acquiring Wilmer Texas, November 2024

The answer arrived in November 2024 in the form of Wilmer, Texas. FREYR Battery announced and closed the acquisition of Trina Solar's US solar module manufacturing operations. The acquisition terms and Section 45X economics are detailed in the Snapshot chapter.

Trina Solar, a major Chinese-origin vertically integrated module producer, had invested in US domestic capacity to serve American utility-scale solar developers requiring domestically manufactured modules for federal and state procurement compliance. The Wilmer facility was operational at acquisition close, meaning FREYR inherited a running production line, an experienced manufacturing workforce, and established customer relationships — a markedly lower-risk entry point than the greenfield gigafactory construction that had defined the Norwegian battery chapter.

> "This acquisition represents a transformational step for our company, positioning us to capitalize on the significant long-term tailwinds in US solar manufacturing supported by the IRA," Barcelo said in the announcement. [T1 Energy press release, November 2024]

The pivot was emphatic. A Norwegian battery start-up had become a Texas solar module manufacturer.

## T1 Energy: Rename, Relocate, Reposition, Q1 2025

The corporate transformation was formalized in the first quarter of 2025 when the company completed a rename to T1 Energy Inc. and changed its NYSE ticker from FREY to TE. The registered headquarters relocated to Austin, Texas — a US domicile consistent with a company whose principal revenue-generating asset sat in the Dallas-Fort Worth corridor.

Norway was retained in the corporate structure but explicitly repositioned. Battery cell development at the Mo i Rana CQP continued at reduced capital intensity — preserved as an option on a longer-cycle battery market recovery rather than as the primary driver of enterprise value or management bandwidth.

## The Strategic Posture at the Pivot's Close

By the spring of 2026, T1 Energy's corporate history had traveled a course unusual even by the turbulent standards of the post-IRA industrial energy transition. Founded as a Nordic clean-power battery play, publicly listed through the SPAC cycle at a moment of peak battery optimism, restructured through the sector's 2023–2024 capital intensity reckoning, and repositioned through a single asset acquisition into US solar module manufacturing — the company's identity had been substantially remade.

The inheritance that defines the forward equity story is Wilmer. The Norwegian battery assets constitute what T1 Energy was — preserved at the margin as a real option, but no longer the reason investors hold the stock or analysts model the cash flows.

chapters.title: Wilmer Texas solar module manufacturing and the residual Norway battery assets
chapters.body:
## Wilmer, Texas: The 5 GW Facility

The Wilmer facility sits in the southern tier of the Dallas metropolitan area, in an industrial corridor that became a node of inbound manufacturing investment during the post-pandemic reshoring cycle. Trina Solar—one of the largest Chinese photovoltaic module manufacturers by global shipment volume and listed on Shanghai's STAR Market—had established the site as part of a broader strategy to access the United States market under the IRA's domestic-content framework. The plant's nameplate capacity of five gigawatts of annual solar module production ranked it among the largest dedicated module-assembly operations in the United States, in a tier below First Solar's Ohio and Alabama thin-film manufacturing infrastructure but ahead of most of the post-IRA entrants that announced capacities in the one-to-three gigawatt range.

The modules produced at Wilmer are built on tunnel oxide passivated contact technology—TOPCon—an n-type silicon architecture that had by late 2024 largely displaced older mono-PERC designs at the performance frontier of mainstream crystalline silicon manufacturing. TOPCon modules typically deliver higher conversion efficiencies than p-type PERC equivalents, with commercial module efficiencies in the 22–23 percent range for leading producers. T1 Energy positioned the Wilmer output as suited for utility-scale ground-mount applications, where module efficiency translates directly into lower balance-of-system cost per delivered watt-hour.

The acquisition was structured to include not just the physical manufacturing infrastructure—production lines, tooling, and inventory—but also the operational workforce and existing customer relationships that Trina Solar US had cultivated. The consideration, inclusive of assumed liabilities, placed the deal at a range the company described in its filings as implying a meaningful discount to the replacement cost of the installed equipment, reflecting both the strategic urgency on Trina's side and the execution risk T1's management was accepting in operating a high-throughput manufacturing facility as an unfamiliar principal.

## Section 45X: The Credit Architecture

The economic logic of the Wilmer acquisition is inseparable from the Section 45X advanced manufacturing production tax credit established under the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022. At Wilmer's nameplate capacity of five gigawatts, a fully utilized module-assembly operation generating module-level credits alone would accumulate approximately $350 million in Section 45X credits annually—a figure that dwarfs the reported acquisition consideration and frames the deal as a credit-stream acquisition as much as a manufacturing one.

| Scenario | Annual GW Produced | 45X Module Credit ($0.07/W) | Annual Credit Value |
|---|---|---|---|
| 20% utilization | 1.0 GW | $0.07 | $70M |
| 40% utilization | 2.0 GW | $0.07 | $140M |
| 80% utilization | 4.0 GW | $0.07 | $280M |
| Full nameplate | 5.0 GW | $0.07 | $350M |

The credits are structured as direct-pay eligible for the first five years of a project's eligibility period, meaning T1 Energy could recover the credits as cash refunds independent of its tax-liability position—a provision of particular value to a company still carrying net losses through the transition period. After the direct-pay window, the credits become transferable, creating a secondary market that solar manufacturers have used to monetize credit streams against third-party tax-equity buyers at modest haircuts to face value.

The critical caveat in the Section 45X framework involves the domestic-content definition for cells. Wilmer's initial operational configuration relied on cell procurement from offshore suppliers, drawing on the broader Trina Solar supply chain. Under that model, the facility qualified for module-level credits only. Full credit stacking—module plus cell, reaching eleven cents per watt combined—would require either establishing domestic cell manufacturing or sourcing cells from US producers, a capital decision management acknowledged as a medium-term option rather than an immediate operational commitment.

## Customer Base and Market Positioning

The customer base inherited from Trina Solar US skewed heavily toward utility-scale solar development, reflecting the scale of Wilmer's output and the difficulty of routing five-gigawatt-per-year production volumes through residential or commercial distribution channels. Utility-scale independent power producers assembling large ground-mount projects across the ERCOT, MISO, and SPP balancing areas formed the core demand channel, with procurement decisions driven by module efficiency specifications, bankability with tax-equity investors, and domestic-content compliance requirements for projects seeking the IRA's investment tax credit adder.

T1 Energy's management signaled interest in the residential solar installer market as a secondary demand channel, though the economics differ materially from utility offtake—shorter production runs, higher logistics cost per watt, more fragmented procurement, and greater sensitivity to brand positioning in a channel where installer relationships and warranty credibility matter alongside module price.

The competitive reference point most directly relevant to T1 Energy's positioning was not First Solar—whose cadmium-telluride thin-film technology and multi-decade US utility-scale installation history occupy a distinct market tier—but rather the South Korean-backed crystalline silicon manufacturers, principally Hanwha Qcells, which established multi-gigawatt US capacity in Dalton, Georgia under comparable IRA economics. Both T1 and Qcells compete for the same utility-scale procurement decisions, with similar TOPCon-era module efficiency profiles, similar credit support, and similar dependence on offshore cell supply pending domestic cell investments.

## Operational Scaling Through 2025

Ramping a five-gigawatt module facility from an acquisition baseline to stable, high-utilization production is a logistical and workforce challenge that the broader US solar manufacturing expansion had navigated with mixed results through 2024. Supply-chain integration—securing cell supply, glass, encapsulant, backsheet, frames, and junction boxes under terms consistent with domestic-content thresholds—was the primary operational bottleneck in the early post-acquisition quarters at Wilmer.

The Dallas corridor location provided access to a deep industrial labor pool and the multimodal logistics infrastructure—interstate highway connectivity, proximity to the Gulf Coast port complex at Houston—that the input volumes of a five-gigawatt operation require. Management communications through 2025 described a trajectory of increasing line utilization as supply relationships were consolidated and the workforce stabilized following the ownership transition.

## Mo i Rana: The Residual Battery Position

Against the operational activity at Wilmer, the Norwegian battery assets registered as a footnote in T1 Energy's investor communications by early 2025—present on the balance sheet, acknowledged in strategic disclosures, but no longer the animating thesis of the equity story.

The Mo i Rana Customer Qualification Plant, constructed at material capital expense through 2022 and 2023, represented a functioning proof of FREYR's manufacturing approach. The CQP was designed to validate the 24M Technologies semi-solid electrode process that FREYR had licensed, producing battery cells at pilot scale for customer qualification purposes.

As of the snapshot date, T1 Energy had not announced a divestiture of the Mo i Rana assets. The posture was one of managed de-prioritization: maintaining the CQP at a reduced activity level, preserving optionality around a potential future battery-industry partner or acquirer, and avoiding the write-down crystallization that an outright distressed sale would force onto the income statement.

chapters.title: Trina acquisition financing, Section 45X PTC economics, and the 2025-2026 ramp
chapters.body:
## A Transaction Priced for Urgency

The acquisition of Trina Solar's Wilmer, Texas manufacturing operations in November 2024 was not a transaction that FREYR Battery spent years engineering. It was an opportunistic pivot executed under duress — and the financial terms reflected that urgency on both sides of the table.

The discount was not incidental. Trina Solar, a Chinese-headquartered manufacturer, faced escalating US tariff and trade-policy risk on Chinese-origin solar products, and the IRA Section 45X credit framework had fundamentally altered the economics of US-domiciled production in ways that favored a buyer with US-resident capital and an NYSE listing. FREYR, for its part, needed a revenue-generating asset and a credible US manufacturing story. The transaction closed the alignment gap between a seller seeking an exit from a US subsidiary and a buyer seeking a transformation thesis.

The Wilmer facility itself was not a greenfield risk. The acquisition transferred the physical plant, the production equipment, the operational team, and the customer relationships. FREYR was not buying a promise; it was buying a running machine.

## SPAC Proceeds, Subsequent Capital, and the Bridge to Wilmer

Understanding how FREYR financed the Trina acquisition requires tracing the capital structure from the July 2021 SPAC merger. The SPAC capital was substantially committed to the Mo i Rana construction program. By 2023, FREYR had joined a cohort of battery pure-plays — Northvolt, Britishvolt, Eos Energy — confronting the reality that scaling battery cell production from demonstration to gigawatt commercial volumes required billions of dollars, not hundreds of millions, and that strategic customers were not prepared to sign offtake at price levels that would support those economics.

The capital structure entering the Trina acquisition was accordingly strained. The company had drawn down against its SPAC proceeds across Mo i Rana construction, US project development costs, corporate overhead, and the Atlanta gigafactory planning effort. Financing the Trina consideration — and the working capital requirements of absorbing a 5-gigawatt operational facility — required incremental capital actions. SEC filings from the late 2024 period detail the bridge financing and equity components arranged to close the Wilmer transaction.

## Section 45X: The Tax Credit That Rewrote the Calculus

The $350 million figure at full utilization is not revenue in the conventional sense — it is a tax attribute that either offsets corporate tax liability or, under IRA transferability rules, can be sold to third-party tax credit buyers at a market discount (typically 90 to 95 cents on the dollar in the transfer market as of 2025). For a company of T1 Energy's scale, the credit value at full ramp would dwarf the underlying manufacturing margin on the modules themselves. In a commodity solar market where module ASPs have compressed toward $0.15 to $0.25 per watt through Chinese overcapacity, a $0.07 per watt domestic production subsidy is not supplemental economics — it is the economics.

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Wilmer nameplate capacity | 5.0 GW |
| Section 45X module credit rate | $0.07/W |
| Implied annual credit at full utilization | ~$350M |
| Credit character | Per-unit production; transferable |
| IRA sunset provision | Phase-down begins 2029 |

The Section 45X framework extends beyond modules. Credits are also available for US-manufactured solar cells ($0.04/W) and wafers, creating an incentive to vertically integrate upstream. Capturing the full cell credit stack would require capital investment in cell manufacturing equipment — a second-phase capex commitment that the company had signaled but not yet formally committed to in filed disclosures.

## FY2025 Revenue Trajectory and the Ramp Profile

The Wilmer facility's revenue trajectory in 2025 depended on two compounding variables: the utilization rate against its 5-gigawatt nameplate, and the realized average selling price for US-manufactured modules in a market still navigating the tension between IRA-supported domestic production and the persistent pricing pressure from Chinese module supply chains operating through Southeast Asian transshipment routes.

The first half of 2025 reflected commissioning discipline — ensuring product qualification with utility-scale customers, aligning supply chain procurement for US-content compliance, and integrating FREYR's corporate infrastructure with the inherited Trina operational team. 

FY2026, by the company's internal framing, is positioned as the first full-year operational scaling period — the year in which the Wilmer facility's utilization rate should more closely approximate nameplate and in which Section 45X credit generation should begin approaching the theoretical $350 million annual ceiling.

## Norway: The Residual Capex Obligation

The Mo i Rana CQP remained on T1 Energy's balance sheet through the snapshot date. The facility's carrying value and associated decommissioning or maintenance obligations appear in T1 Energy's SEC filings; the capital required to advance Mo i Rana to any form of commercial production would be substantial — likely in the hundreds of millions of dollars — and the company's disclosed capital allocation priority had unmistakably shifted toward Wilmer.

The practical effect of maintaining the Norway assets is a modest but persistent drag on corporate resources — facility costs, a reduced Norwegian workforce, intellectual property licensing obligations to 24M Technologies — against the theoretical optionality of a future battery business. The strategic hierarchy was unambiguous: Wilmer first, Norway a distant and contingent second.

chapters.title: Pre-pivot FREYR quarters through Trina acquisition and post-rename ramp
chapters.body:
## The Battery Thesis, Intact — Until It Wasn't

When FREYR AS closed its business combination with Alussa Energy Acquisition Corp. on July 9, 2021, the Norwegian lithium-ion startup arrived on the New York Stock Exchange with a pro forma equity value of $1.4 billion, a $600 million PIPE, and a thesis premised on the conviction that clean battery cell manufacturing could be scaled into a globally competitive enterprise. The ambition was explicit: FREYR would build Giga Arctic in Mo i Rana, Norway, using the licensed 24M Technologies SemiSolid™ platform, and pair it with an American manufacturing footprint. In November 2022 the company announced the purchase of a 368-acre site in Coweta County, Georgia — Giga America — with an initial capital investment estimate of $1.7 billion and a preliminary target of 34 GWh of annual cell production capacity.

The quarterly cadence through 2022 and into 2023 tracked two parallel narratives: progress at the Customer Qualification Plant in Mo i Rana, and capital planning for the Georgia site. Neither moved as fast as the equity story had promised. For the full year ended December 31, 2022, FREYR reported a net loss of $98.8 million, or $0.83 per diluted share, with revenue still effectively nil. The company had capital but no product.

## The C-Suite Revolving Door

The strategic tension produced leadership turbulence. In August 2023 the company announced that co-founder and chief executive Tom Einar Jensen would become Executive Chair, with Birger Steen — a technology sector veteran with stints leading Microsoft's operations in Norway and Russia — installed as CEO. Torstein Dale Sjøtveit, FREYR's founding Executive Chair, retired on the same date. Steen lasted ten months. By June 2024, Jensen was reinstated as chief executive, Steen departed from both the CEO seat and the board, and Daniel Barcelo — a director on the FREYR board — was elevated to Chair. Evan Calio was named CFO concurrently.

For the full year ended December 31, 2023, FREYR reported a net loss of $71.9 million, or $0.51 per diluted share — a narrowing versus 2022 that reflected aggressive cost rationalisation rather than revenue progress. Year-end cash stood at $276 million. Management projected a two-year liquidity runway on a reduced-burn basis. The Giga America capex estimate had by then grown to $2.6 billion; the Giga Arctic milestone targets had been quietly pushed back. In Norway, 78 employees and contractors were laid off as part of a restructuring that cut the management layer from 19 directors to six. The company described its posture as "FREYR 2.0."

## Barcelo Takes Command

The definition arrived in the autumn of 2024. Daniel Barcelo assumed the chief executive role from Jensen, who was appointed CEO of FREYR Europe to oversee the "optimization and monetization" of the European portfolio — a diplomatic formulation for an orderly wind-down.

On November 6, 2024, FREYR announced the acquisition of Trina Solar's US manufacturing assets. The Wilmer facility had commenced production on November 1, 2024 — five days before the announcement. Line 1 was operational; commissioning on Line 2 had begun. The full seven-line facility was targeting production ramp through H2 2025. Thirty percent of estimated production volumes were backed by firm US customer offtake contracts. The transaction closed on December 24, 2024.

## The Rename and the Reckoning with Georgia

Barcelo's strategic reorientation completed its symbolic arc on February 19, 2025, when the company filed to change its corporate name from FREYR Battery Inc. to **T1 Energy Inc.** Common stock and warrants ceased trading under FREY and FREY WS on March 3, 2025, and commenced as TE and TE WS on the New York Stock Exchange.

Nine days before the rename, on February 10, 2025, came the formal admission that Giga America was finished. The company announced the sale of its Coweta County, Georgia site to an undisclosed buyer for gross proceeds of $50 million — netting $22.5 million after repayment of state and local grants. The project, which had grown from a $1.7 billion original plan to a $2.6 billion total investment estimate, was attributed by the company to "rising interest rates, falling battery prices, changes in management, and a realignment of the company's near-term strategic goals." The six-year battery cell chapter was closed.

> "The rebirth of our company as T1 Energy is about American energy, jobs, and advanced manufacturing. The U.S. needs domestic supply chains and manufacturing capacity to harness its abundant solar resources. T1 is committed to building that capacity," Barcelo said at the rename. "More than 80% of new U.S. electricity capacity in 2024 was solar and batteries. T1 plans to lead in the solar and battery markets by enabling the growth in energy supply required to support AI, data centers, reshoring, and electrification — to restore American industrial capacity and leadership in future advanced industries."

## Post-Rename Ramp: The First Year

FY2024 had recorded only $2.9 million in consolidated revenue against a net loss of $450.2 million — the bulk of the loss attributable to pre-acquisition wind-down costs and the Norwegian portfolio write-downs.

The trajectory was constructive but complicated. In mid-2025, T1 revised its full-year production plan downward from 3.4 GW to 2.6–3.0 GW, citing the need to accommodate trade and industrial policy uncertainty, production line technology conversions, and the ramp of new sales initiatives beyond the Trina offtake. Year-end unrestricted cash was $182.5 million, with an adjusted EBITDA of negative $65.0 million.

| Period | Revenue (USD) | Net Loss (USD) | Module Production |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2022 | Negligible | $98.8M | — (battery CQP) |
| FY2023 | Negligible | $71.9M | — (battery CQP) |
| FY2024 | $2.9M | $450.2M | Transition year |
| Q1 2025 | $64.6M | — | 443 MW |
| FY2025 | $755.3M | $380.8M | 2.79 GW |

The company entered 2026 guiding production of 3.1 to 4.2 GW and targeting a G2 domestic cell manufacturing facility — site selection completed in Q1 2025, construction originally targeted mid-2025 — that would deepen the vertical integration story FREYR's Norwegian founders once told about batteries.

chapters.title: Daniel Barcelo, Trina-inherited operational leadership, and the post-rename board
chapters.body:
## From Founder to Subsidiary: Tom Einar Jensen's Receding Arc

When FREYR Battery went public via the Alussa Energy SPAC in July 2021, Tom Einar Jensen was the face and founding logic of the enterprise. Jensen had co-founded FREYR AS in 2018 alongside Torstein Dale Sjøtveit, who retired from the company's leadership in the course of the 2023 succession that would mark the beginning of FREYR's long leadership turbulence.

The battery industry's capital-intensity reset made Jensen's CEO position progressively untenable. In August 2023, he transitioned to Executive Chair of the Board, and Birger Steen — a Norwegian technology-sector executive — was brought in to execute what the board described as an accelerated path toward profitability. Steen lasted ten months. In June 2024, Steen and CFO Oscar Brown departed within hours of each other. Steen's exit was framed by the board in purely strategic terms; Steen alone collected a NOK 7 million severance.

Jensen returned to the CEO role in June 2024 on an interim basis while the board simultaneously restructured its own upper tier. Daniel Barcelo was appointed Chair. Evan Calio was named CFO. The arrangement was understood by the market as a bridge position: Jensen was the continuity vehicle while the board negotiated the Trina Solar asset acquisition.

When the Trina deal was announced November 5, 2024, Barcelo was installed as CEO the following day. Jensen stepped down from the T1 Energy board and accepted the position of CEO of FREYR Europe, the subsidiary retaining oversight of the Mo i Rana battery cell assets. His shareholding — approximately 2.8 million shares carried through the transition — maintained financial alignment with the renamed enterprise even as his operating authority narrowed.

## Daniel Barcelo: Capital-Markets Operator in a Manufacturing Chair

Barcelo, 56 at the time of his November 2024 appointment, arrived at T1 Energy's executive office via energy finance rather than energy production. He had been a portfolio manager at Moore Capital Management, one of the pre-crisis era's most prominent macro hedge funds. Before Moore, he served as a Senior Research Analyst in oil and gas at Bank of America, and as a Director and Senior Analyst in the same sector at Lehman Brothers. A tenure as Managing Director and Head of Oil and Gas at Renaissance Capital in Moscow gave him direct exposure to the Russian energy complex at a moment of peak Western institutional interest in that market.

Barcelo also held operating-level financial roles: Chief Financial Officer of Ruspetro plc, a Russia-focused upstream oil producer listed in London; Head of Corporate Finance at Lekoil Limited, an E&P company active in Nigeria; co-founder and CFO of Invicti Terra Argentina Limited, a Latin American energy development vehicle. He is a CFA charterholder with a BS in Finance from Syracuse University.

At T1 Energy, that résumé maps most directly to the single most consequential near-term management challenge: not manufacturing yield optimization but the monetization of Section 45X advanced manufacturing production tax credits — a structured-finance exercise requiring credibility with institutional tax-equity buyers. Barcelo's public statements since the rename have consistently framed T1's thesis in supply-chain integration terms rather than module-level cost competition:

> "We are building something that does not exist in the U.S. today — an integrated, secure, traceable polysilicon-based supply chain."

## Joseph Evan Calio: The CFO Pairing

Joseph Evan Calio, appointed CFO on June 13, 2024, as part of the same leadership reset that brought Barcelo to Chair, carried a career trajectory that closely paralleled his CEO's. Calio had been a Managing Director covering Energy and Infrastructure investment banking at BTIG; before that, he spent fourteen years at Morgan Stanley as a Managing Director in equity research covering E&P companies, refiners, and integrated oils. He holds a BS from Lehigh University, a JD from Widener University School of Law, and an LLM from Georgetown University Law Center — a combination suggesting the tax and structured-finance literacy that T1's Section 45X credit sales will continue to demand. Calio received a 666,666 RSU grant vesting ratably over three years, anchoring his economic interest through the stated 2027 operational target of 5 GW of integrated production between the G1 Dallas and G2 Austin facilities.

## Operational Continuity: The FREYR Engineering Thread

One executive who bridged the Norwegian founding and the Texas build-out was Einar GS Kilde, who had served as Chief Operating Officer of FREYR AS since October 2019 — predating the SPAC listing and representing the deepest institutional memory of the Mo i Rana construction years. His title evolved to Chief Development Officer as the company's capital deployment shifted to the G2 Austin solar cell facility. He retired from T1 Energy in April 2026, closing out the last of the original FREYR engineering leadership from the parent-company executive suite.

Beneath that layer, Barcelo assembled a functional team that included Jaime Gualy as Executive Vice President of Corporate Development, Andy Munro as Chief Legal Officer, and Russell Gold as Executive Vice President of Strategic Communications — a configuration reflecting both the external presentation demands of a post-SPAC NYSE company and the specific Washington visibility that an IRA-era domestic manufacturing story commands.

## Board Architecture: Holdovers, the Trina Designee, and the Post-Rename Refresh

The board T1 Energy carried through the February 2025 rename was predominantly a FREYR Battery–era construction. The nine directors elected at the June 2025 annual meeting included the chairman-CEO Barcelo and a contingent of independent directors whose appointments traced to the 2021–2024 FREYR period.

| Director | Background | Board tenure origin |
|---|---|---|
| Daniel Barcelo | Moore Capital / Lehman / Ruspetro CFO; Chairman & CEO | Nov. 2024 (appointment as CEO) |
| W. Richard Anderson | Former CFO/CEO Prime Natural Resources; former CFO Eurasia Drilling | FREYR-era, 2024 |
| Todd Jason Kantor | Founder, Encompass Capital Advisors (long/short energy equity, 25 years) | FREYR-era, 2024 |
| David J. Manners | Founder, Decapolis Group; 20-year CIA career including multiple Chief of Station postings | FREYR-era, SPAC period |
| Peter Matrai | EDGE Global LLC; ~2.4M shares; ongoing consulting role | FREYR-era, SPAC period |
| Daniel Steingart | Stanley-Thompson Professor of Chemical Metallurgy, Columbia University; Co-Director, Columbia Electrochemical Energy Center | FREYR-era, Jan. 2023 |
| Jessica Wirth Strine | CEO, Sustainable Governance Partners; former BlackRock and Vanguard portfolio manager | FREYR-era, Nov. 2023 |
| Robert Hammond | Director of IR–North America, TotalEnergies, 1994–2023 | Post-rename, March 2026 |

The Trina Solar acquisition had added one designated seat: Mingxing "Charles" Lin, Trina Solar's Chief Strategy Officer with nearly twenty years in multinational finance and management, who joined in December 2024 as Trina's contractual board designee. His presence formalized the former Chinese manufacturer's continuing equity stake in the renamed enterprise.

Lin's directorship proved short-lived. In late March 2026, both Lin and Tore Ivar Slettemoen — a Norwegian industrial entrepreneur with over 4.1 million shares held through Teknovekst entities, representing one of the largest individual ownership positions on the board — resigned simultaneously. The company stated neither departure arose from disagreements over operations or policy. Hammond, who had spent nearly thirty years managing investor relations for TotalEnergies's North American operations, was elected to fill one of the vacated seats and was placed on both the Audit and Risk Committee and the Compensation Committee.

The board configuration as of the May 2026 snapshot had shed the Trina Solar designee, the founding-era Norwegian anchor shareholder, and the last formal instruments of the battery-company governance era. What replaced them was a director table weighted toward US energy-sector capital-markets fluency — closely mirroring the Barcelo-Calio executive pairing and telegraphing where T1 Energy intended to source its next phase of institutional credibility as the G2 Austin solar cell facility moved toward its targeted 2026 production start.

chapters.title: US solar developers, polysilicon and wafer supply, and the Norway battery upstream
chapters.body:
## The Customer Base: US Utility-Scale Solar

The Wilmer facility supplies a customer base drawn principally from the US independent power producer community — project sponsors and engineering, procurement, and construction contractors for whom IRA domestic content eligibility is a material project-finance consideration.

The structural commercial driver is the domestic content bonus adder under Sections 48 and 45Y of the IRA: projects qualifying under Treasury's domestic content guidance for steel, iron, and manufactured products access an additional 10-percentage-point bonus on the base tax credit. For a utility-scale project financed on tax-equity terms, that adder materially reshapes project IRRs. T1 Energy's Wilmer-manufactured modules are positioned — subject to the cell content rules discussed below — to qualify as US-manufactured products, creating a direct commercial link between the IRA's domestic content incentive architecture and Wilmer's order book.

The broader utility-scale US solar installation pipeline ran at roughly 30 GW annually through 2024-2025. Beyond utility-scale developers, the Wilmer facility's module specifications are compatible with commercial and community solar applications, though the company's disclosed commercial focus has centred on the large-project procurement channel where domestic content value is most directly monetised.

## Polysilicon and Wafer: The China Upstream Dependency

The critical upstream constraint at Wilmer is cells and wafers. Standard crystalline silicon module manufacturing requires a supply chain running from polysilicon through ingot to wafer to cell before module assembly — and as of the Trina acquisition, Wilmer was configured for module assembly, not cell production. Cell procurement is therefore the decisive upstream exposure.

China accounts for roughly 80-90 percent of global polysilicon, wafer, and cell manufacturing capacity. The leading Chinese cell producers — Tongwei, LONGi Green Energy, JA Solar, and Trina Solar itself — operate at cost structures that nascent US-based cell manufacturing cannot yet replicate at comparable scale absent subsidy support.

The US polysilicon base remains thin. Hemlock Semiconductor, headquartered in Hemlock, Michigan, is the primary domestic polysilicon producer. REC Silicon — the Norwegian polysilicon manufacturer with a facility in Butte, Montana — has faced recurring operational constraints. Neither producer offers polysilicon at the scale or pricing comparable to Chinese counterparts, and no meaningful vertically integrated ingot, wafer, or cell manufacturing capacity exists in the US today at the volume T1 Energy would require.

| Upstream input | Current US capacity | Key domestic suppliers | Estimated China global share |
|---|---|---|---|
| Polysilicon | Limited | Hemlock Semiconductor; REC Silicon (Butte, MT) | ~85% |
| Ingot / Wafer | Minimal | — | ~95%+ |
| Solar cells | Early-stage | Hanwha Q CELLS (Dalton, GA); planned expansions | ~85% |
| Modules | Growing | First Solar; T1 Energy/Wilmer; Hanwha Q CELLS; Silfab | Expanding US share post-IRA |

For T1 Energy, building an IRA-compliant and FEOC-clean upstream supply chain over the medium term means either sourcing cells from the small number of US cell manufacturers, contracting with non-FEOC-designated country suppliers — Hanwha Q CELLS' Dalton, Georgia cell facility is the most significant non-Chinese domestic cell source — or procuring through Southeast Asian or Indian producers whose supply chains can satisfy the domestic content test in the near-term transition period. The latter carries trade litigation exposure.

## The Trina Solar Relationship: Former Parent, Residual Supplier

The commercial and technical relationship between T1 Energy and Trina Solar did not sever cleanly at closing. Trina Solar retained its global manufacturing operations, technology platform, and brand; what transferred was the US manufacturing footprint and associated assets. Transition services agreements customary in carve-out transactions would govern near-term operational continuity.

The cell supply question intersects directly with the Trina relationship in a manner that creates ongoing compliance complexity. If Trina Solar remained a cell supplier to Wilmer post-acquisition, the arrangement would expose T1 Energy to the same Chinese supply chain risk that constrains IRA domestic content eligibility and raises FEOC exposure as Treasury and DOE tighten the foreign entity of concern rules. Trina Solar's corporate structure and any PRC state-linked ownership interests are a material due diligence variable.

T1 Energy's management has publicly characterised the Wilmer facility as targeting a domestically compliant supply chain over time — a managed migration away from Chinese-origin cell supply rather than an immediate severance, paralleling the IRA's own phase-in schedule for FEOC restrictions.

## US-China Trade Policy: Tariff Architecture and UFLPA Exposure

The US solar import tariff regime has been in effective force since the Obama administration's antidumping and countervailing duty orders on Chinese crystalline silicon products, with the Section 201 safeguard tariff layer added in January 2018. The Biden administration largely maintained the architecture while adding complexity: a June 2022 presidential proclamation waived Section 201 tariffs on imports from Malaysia, Vietnam, Cambodia, and Thailand for 24 months, while simultaneously initiating circumvention investigations.

The framework entering T1 Energy's 2025 operational period was one in which cells and modules of Chinese origin — or of Southeast Asian origin adjudged to circumvent existing orders — faced combined AD/CVD and Section 201 duty exposure exceeding 40-50 percent across most product categories. The Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act, effective June 2022, layered a rebuttable presumption of forced labour for goods with any Xinjiang nexus; a substantial proportion of Chinese polysilicon has historically been produced in or processed through Xinjiang, creating documentary compliance requirements that Chinese suppliers have been inconsistent in satisfying.

For T1 Energy, this tariff and compliance environment simultaneously constitutes the economic moat supporting Wilmer's viability and the supply chain constraint limiting upstream optionality. Domestically manufactured modules avoid tariff burden and UFLPA exposure entirely. The constraint is procuring upstream inputs — cells above all — at competitive cost while maintaining supply chain traceability documentation.

## Norway: The Battery Upstream That Persists

The battery upstream exposure at Mo i Rana is structurally analogous to Wilmer's solar supply challenge: lithium, nickel, manganese, and cobalt for NMC chemistry cells are similarly concentrated in supply chains with dominant Chinese processing. The IRA's FEOC restrictions, applied to battery components under Section 45X and Section 48C, create parallel sourcing constraints, with tightening schedules that make non-Chinese battery raw material supply increasingly necessary for credit eligibility.

The Norway assets represent an optionality position on a battery market recovery rather than an active capital deployment programme — retaining residual value as a developed industrial site with existing regulatory approvals, without commanding meaningful near-term investment priority against Wilmer's Section 45X-supported economics.

chapters.title: Where T1 Energy sits against First Solar and the US solar module manufacturing build-out
chapters.body:
The US solar module manufacturing landscape that T1 Energy entered through its November 2024 acquisition was not a greenfield opportunity. The field already had a clear dominant player, a cohort of well-capitalized Korean-backed entrants, and a policy architecture — IRA Section 45X — that rewarded incumbency. The question was whether a company with a roughly $100–200 million entry ticket and a 5-gigawatt facility originally built by one of China's largest panel producers could carve out defensible ground.

## First Solar: The Benchmark No One Touches

No analysis of US solar module manufacturing begins anywhere other than First Solar. The Tempe, Arizona–headquartered company spent two decades building a cadmium-telluride thin-film manufacturing capability that no competitor has replicated at commercial scale. By the time IRA Section 45X took effect, First Solar was already generating advanced manufacturing production credits on a production base expanding toward 10 gigawatts of annual US nameplate capacity, distributed across facilities in Perrysburg, Ohio and a newer Alabama factory that came online in 2024. CdTe panels carry temperature coefficients that perform advantageously at utility-scale installations in high-irradiance, high-heat US markets, and they carry no exposure to the polysilicon supply chains that have drawn UFLPA scrutiny.

First Solar's balance sheet entering 2025 reflected those advantages. The company had accumulated substantial Section 45X credit flows while carrying a net cash position that gave it financial flexibility no new entrant could match. Its customer roster was dominated by long-duration utility-scale power purchase agreements with investment-grade offtakers. For T1 Energy, First Solar represented the ceiling of what US-headquartered solar module manufacturing could aspire to.

## The Korean Entrants and the Crystalline-Silicon Field

T1 Energy's more immediate competitive universe was the cluster of crystalline-silicon module manufacturers drawing on 45X credits to bridge the cost gap with overseas production. Hanwha Q CELLS, the US subsidiary of South Korea's Hanwha Solutions, committed roughly $2.5 billion to a Cartersville, Georgia facility that scaled toward approximately 8 gigawatts of annual module capacity. Hanwha brought Korean balance-sheet depth, existing utility-scale customer relationships, and the ability to integrate a domestic cell manufacturing line that unlocked the cell-level 45X credit on top of the module-level credit. That stacked credit capture — $0.04 per watt for cells plus $0.07 per watt for modules — was a meaningful economics differentiator for manufacturers able to produce both.

Silfab Solar, the Canadian-headquartered manufacturer with US production in Monroe, Washington, operated at smaller scale but with established Pacific Northwest customer relationships and a manufacturing pedigree predating the IRA incentive cycle. Heliene, another Canadian-headquartered producer, similarly held US production positions. Further down the capacity curve, a broader cohort of announced US manufacturing projects was navigating an uncertain regulatory environment as Treasury issued domestic content bonus adder guidance.

## T1's Inherited Footprint and the Trina Provenance Question

The Wilmer plant was purpose-built by Trina Solar to serve US customers from a domestically domiciled production base. Trina's decision to divest rather than continue operating through a trade-sensitive period reflected the complexity of Chinese-parent-company exposure under an increasingly stringent US trade and investment review framework.

The 5-gigawatt nameplate at Wilmer positioned T1, at full run-rate, as the second-largest US solar module manufacturer by stated capacity — a striking fact for a company that had been a Norwegian battery startup eighteen months prior. But nameplate capacity and actual shipped gigawatts are distinct quantities. As of the snapshot date, T1 was ramping production rather than operating at full utilization.

| Manufacturer | Technology | Approx. US Capacity (GW) | Domestic Cell Production |
|---|---|---|---|
| First Solar | CdTe thin-film | ~10+ | Yes (integrated) |
| Hanwha Q CELLS | TOPCon / PERC | ~8 | Yes (Cartersville) |
| T1 Energy | TOPCon | ~5 | No |
| Silfab Solar | Mono PERC / TOPCon | ~2 | Limited |

The absence of domestic cell production at Wilmer was a competitive gap with direct financial consequences. US TOPCon cells were in constrained domestic supply, leaving T1 dependent on imported cells. That dependency had two compounding effects: it reduced 45X credit capture to the module level only, and it created supply-chain exposure to any additional trade actions targeting cell imports. A domestic cell line would add a further $200 million at full run-rate, underscoring the gap between T1's current configuration and the vertically integrated economics Hanwha was assembling in Georgia.

## The 45X Equalizer and the Trade Policy Moat

Section 45X was the reason the US solar module manufacturing competitive landscape looked as it did entering 2025. The advanced manufacturing production credit made domestic production economics viable at a time when Chinese manufacturers could produce modules at costs no US facility could approach in a purely market-driven framework. For all the competitive differences between First Solar's proprietary thin-film technology, Hanwha's stacked-credit TOPCon modules, and T1's Wilmer facility, the 45X credit was the shared foundation on which each company's US manufacturing business case rested.

That shared dependency was also a shared policy risk. The IRA Section 45X credit was written through 2032, with phase-downs beginning in 2030, but the legislative environment remained subject to political change. For T1 Energy — a company that had staked its entire post-pivot strategic identity on the Trina acquisition and 45X-supported US solar manufacturing — that policy dependency was the governing variable of the investment case.

chapters.title: From 2018 founding through SPAC, Atlanta reset, Trina, and T1 rename
chapters.body:
## The Corporate Arc in Retrospect

FREYR Battery was incorporated in 2018 by Norwegian entrepreneur Tom Einar Jensen, who had identified a European strategic gap in lithium-ion manufacturing capacity. The company was registered in Luxembourg — a structure that gave it European legal standing and capital market optionality — while retaining its operational and cultural identity as a Norwegian enterprise centred on Mo i Rana.

The path to US public markets ran through the 2020–2021 SPAC wave. By mid-2024, after the battery thesis collided with capital intensity realities and Chinese cost competition, Daniel Barcelo succeeded Jensen as CEO. The Trina Solar acquisition followed in November 2024, and the corporate transformation to T1 Energy Inc. was formalized in Q1 2025.

## Forward Catalysts

The post-rename operational agenda centres on three near-term tests:

**Wilmer Texas production ramp**: The facility was operational at acquisition, but scaling throughput against the 5 GW nameplate requires sustained customer commitments, supply chain integration, and manufacturing yield optimisation across module assembly lines inherited from Trina's prior ownership.

**Section 45X credit realisation**: The $0.07/W module credit is non-refundable but transferable under IRA provisions. T1's ability to monetise credits efficiently — whether through direct tax liability offset or transferability sales to third-party buyers — will materially determine the 2025 and 2026 reported economics.

**Customer expansion**: The US solar module supply landscape is consolidating around a small number of domestic manufacturers, with First Solar the dominant scaled competitor. T1's ability to secure utility-scale supply agreements with power developers and independent power producers represents the critical commercial execution test.

## The Mo i Rana Question

The residual Mo i Rana strategic posture remains the most structurally ambiguous element of the T1 Energy investment thesis. The Norwegian asset is neither wound down nor actively capitalised — its resolution through sale, joint venture, or eventual restart under different market conditions remained an open strategic question as of the snapshot date.

chapters.title: Solar module technology, residual battery IP, and the Section 45X compliance framework
chapters.body:
When T1 Energy inherited the Wilmer, Texas manufacturing complex from Trina Solar in November 2024, it acquired not merely a 5-gigawatt nameplate capacity but a complete manufacturing lineage in tunnel oxide passivated contact technology — TOPCon — one of the highest-efficiency crystalline-silicon cell architectures in commercial production.

## TOPCon at Wilmer: Competitive Positioning

Trina Solar, which established the Wilmer facility as its primary US manufacturing footprint, had invested in TOPCon production lines as part of a global shift toward next-generation cell architectures. When FREYR Battery closed the acquisition, the Wilmer complex carried Trina's process recipes, equipment calibrations, and ongoing supply relationships. T1 Energy's stated task was to operate and expand that infrastructure rather than to redesign it — a critical distinction that reduced technical ramp risk relative to greenfield module development.

The multi-year efficiency and reliability documentation inherited from Trina carries material commercial value: project finance lenders require bankable performance history for module procurement, and a validated lineage shortens the qualification cycle for new buyers.

## Section 45X: Compliance Architecture

Compliance with Section 45X imposes rigorous production documentation requirements. The manufacturer must substantiate unit output volumes, demonstrate that modules were produced at a qualifying US facility, and satisfy Treasury guidance distinguishing genuine domestic production from final assembly of substantially imported subcomponents. The Trina-inherited manufacturing process was architected to meet a high bar of domestic value-add. Trina Solar had anticipated IRA-era incentives when developing the facility, and that forward planning provided T1 with a compliance infrastructure already calibrated to the relevant regulatory standard. Post-acquisition, T1's internal compliance team assumed responsibility for the full documentation chain: production and yield logs, equipment provenance records, intercompany supply documentation, and audit trails sufficient for IRS examination.

The 45X module credit phases down beginning in 2030, declining ten percent per year and reaching full expiration for most components by 2032. That sunset creates a defined cash-flow window that concentrates the financial argument for Wilmer in the period from 2025 through 2029 and reinforces the near-term operational imperative to maximise throughput while the credit is intact.

## The Mo i Rana Legacy: Battery IP and Strategic Optionality

FREYR Battery's founding thesis was organised around a licensed manufacturing process from 24M Technologies, the MIT-affiliated developer of semi-solid lithium-ion electrode technology. 24M's approach — suspending active electrode materials in a liquid slurry rather than casting dry electrode films — was designed to reduce capital cost per gigawatt-hour relative to conventional lithium-ion cell production architectures. FREYR's Customer Qualification Plant at Mo i Rana operationalised that licence in a production context, generating proprietary process data across cell formation cycling, electrolyte filling protocols, and quality control yield curves.

With the strategic pivot to US solar manufacturing, the Mo i Rana intellectual property portfolio entered a period of reduced capital intensity. T1 Energy had not divested the Norwegian assets or publicly terminated the 24M licensing relationship as of May 2026. The CQP data — cell performance characterisation under various formation protocols, yield curve analysis across chemistries, and manufacturing cost benchmarks — represents a body of knowledge whose commercial value depends entirely on whether T1 eventually chooses to license, sell, or reactivate that battery manufacturing pathway.

The asymmetry is notable from an investor perspective. The battery IP consumes management bandwidth and some residual carrying cost while contributing no near-term operating revenue. If the economics of semi-solid battery manufacturing re-emerge as a commercial proposition, T1 holds a documented technical position that would be materially costly to rebuild from scratch.

chapters.title: Trina integration, Section 45X framework continuity, First Solar competition, Norway battery resolution
chapters.body:
## Wilmer, Texas: Integration and the Execution Gap

The most proximate risk facing T1 Energy is whether the company can successfully absorb and scale the Wilmer manufacturing operations. T1 Energy did not build this plant; it acquired a going concern mid-cycle, with embedded procurement relationships, vendor contracts, and workforce dynamics that were originally calibrated to Trina Solar's balance sheet and corporate priorities.

The principal mitigant is that Wilmer had been operational pre-close, and T1 inherited the manufacturing floor in running condition. Yet the history of US clean-energy manufacturing acquisitions is littered with cautionary examples of acquirers who overestimated their capacity to absorb upstream operational complexity while simultaneously managing a corporate rebranding. Integration and rebranding simultaneously is a management bandwidth test. FY2025 is the first real data point; FY2026 will be the first full-year operational stress test.

## Section 45X: The Credit That Runs the Math

The risk is legislative and political. Section 45X, as enacted under the IRA, runs through 2032 — but the history of US energy tax policy is one of extensions, phase-downs, and periodic congressional uncertainty. A future Congress could amend the credit schedule, introduce domestic content recapture provisions, or subject the framework to reconciliation-driven modification. The 2025 federal budget environment, in which IRA provisions became a recurring target in fiscal negotiations, underscored that no statutory sunset guarantee is politically insulated.

The mitigant is structural: Section 45X is a production tax credit that accrues only on actual manufactured output, making it harder to retroactively claw back from operating manufacturers than a forward-looking subsidy. US solar module manufacturing has accumulated a political constituency that crosses party lines in Sun Belt states. Wilmer, Texas sits in a state whose congressional delegation has demonstrated pragmatic support for domestic manufacturing incentives. The concern is the tail risk: a 2027 or 2028 amendment that phases the credit down earlier than 2032 would compress the economic window that justified the Trina acquisition price.

## First Solar and the Competitive Field

T1 Energy does not compete in a vacuum. First Solar (FSLR) is the dominant US solar module pure-play — a manufacturer with a decade-plus head start in thin-film cadmium telluride technology, a balance sheet measured in billions, and a multi-gigawatt US capacity expansion already underway. First Solar's proprietary CdTe technology is outside the crystalline silicon supply chain that connects most US module manufacturers to Asian upstream inputs, giving it structural insulation from certain tariff dynamics that affect silicon-based producers.

| Metric | First Solar (FSLR) | T1 Energy (TE) |
|---|---|---|
| US module technology | CdTe thin-film | Crystalline silicon |
| US manufacturing capacity | Multi-GW, expanding | 5 GW Wilmer (acquired) |
| Section 45X eligibility | Yes | Yes |
| Supply chain upstream exposure | Low (proprietary) | Moderate (silicon supply chain) |
| Balance sheet scale | Multi-billion USD | Smaller-cap acquirer |

The competitive concern is not that First Solar displaces T1 Energy from the US market — demand for domestically manufactured modules is broad enough to sustain multiple producers. The concern is on customer mix and pricing discipline. A smaller-balance-sheet acquirer in the early years of an integration faces more customer qualification friction than an established manufacturer. T1 must demonstrate production reliability and financial staying power to win and retain the off-take relationships that make multi-year capacity meaningful.

## Norway: The Asset That Needs a Resolution

The Mo i Rana battery assets remain on T1 Energy's books at reduced priority. The risk is capital drag and management distraction. Every dollar and every executive hour directed at Norway is a dollar and hour not directed at Wilmer scaling.

The mitigant — if the Norway asset can be monetized, partnered, or resolved — is that resolution would clean the balance sheet and sharpen the investment narrative. The concern is that the Norwegian battery asset, in a market deeply skeptical of greenfield lithium-ion gigafactory capital intensity, may be difficult to divest at a value that avoids a material write-down.

## US Trade Policy and the Chinese Tariff Architecture

Silicon-based US solar module manufacturing sits at the intersection of IRA industrial policy and a volatile trade environment with Chinese producers. The US solar module market has operated under successive tariff regimes — Section 201 safeguard tariffs, Section 301 tariffs, and the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act's supply chain tracing requirements. These measures collectively create a tariff umbrella that elevates the price floor for imported modules, to the benefit of US domestic manufacturers.

The risk is reversal or renegotiation. A US-China trade détente that softened the tariff architecture would compress the price premium available to domestic manufacturers. Separately, a future UFLPA enforcement softening could reduce the compliance burden that currently disadvantages imports. T1 benefits from the current regime; it has limited ability to influence its continuation.

## Capital Structure: The Adequacy Question

The post-acquisition balance sheet carries the obligations of FREYR's battery development history plus the new integration commitments. The central question is whether T1 has sufficient liquidity runway to reach the phase where Section 45X credits are flowing at scale.

A slower-than-planned ramp, a customer contract delay, or an unexpected capital expenditure at the facility could create a financing need in a market that has already demonstrated its willingness to punish SPAC-heritage energy transition companies on dilutive equity raises. The mitigant is that Wilmer is not greenfield — the facility's operational base should generate cash earlier than a construction-stage project. But until the P&L from consolidated Wilmer operations is visible across multiple quarters, the adequacy of the capital structure remains an open analytical question.

chapters.title: Wilmer Texas scaling, Section 45X capture, and the 2026-2030 horizon
chapters.body:
## The Arithmetic of Wilmer

By the time T1 Energy published its first full-year results under the new banner, the strategic logic of the Wilmer Texas acquisition had compressed into a single line of arithmetic. A 5-gigawatt solar module factory operating at capacity against a Section 45X credit of $0.07 per watt generates roughly $350 million annually in direct federal credits — before a single dollar of module revenue. For a company that had spent most of its public life explaining why Norwegian lithium-ion battery cell manufacturing would eventually earn returns, the simplicity was almost disarming.

Unlike the Mo i Rana Customer Qualification Plant, which had absorbed years of capital expenditure before producing a commercially meaningful cell, Wilmer was manufacturing modules before the ink dried on the purchase agreement. That operational inheritance was the core of the acquisition's appeal.

## Section 45X: The Phase-Down Clock

The credit runs at $0.07 per watt of nameplate capacity through 2029, stepping down thereafter: 75 percent in 2030, 50 percent in 2031, 25 percent in 2032, and zero beyond that. Credits attach to production, not to sales, meaning T1 Energy accrues the PTC value at the point of manufacture rather than upon module delivery — a structural advantage that insulates the economics from short-term module pricing pressure.

| Facility capacity | Credit rate (2025-2029) | Implied annual PTC at full output |
|---|---|---|
| 5 GW (nameplate) | $0.07/W | ~$350M/year |
| 3 GW (partial ramp) | $0.07/W | ~$210M/year |
| 1.5 GW (early ramp) | $0.07/W | ~$105M/year |

The step-down schedule gives T1 Energy a compressed window. Full-capacity production in 2026 and 2027 captures the maximum per-watt credit at scale. Each year of delayed ramp-up is not merely a missed revenue quarter — it is a permanent reduction in the credit-weighted value of the investment thesis.

## Ramp Trajectory and Execution Risk

FY2026 marked the first year in which Barcelo's management had full-year ownership of the production schedule and the full-year Section 45X credit accrual. Investors watching the quarterly cadence were tracking utilisation rates against the nameplate 5 GW ceiling, and the pace of that ascent defined the near-term investment case.

The manufacturing challenge at Wilmer is less technological than logistical. Solar module assembly — tabbing, stringing, lamination, framing — is capital-light relative to cell and wafer production. The constraint is upstream. Trina's original Wilmer operation sourced cells from its own Chinese manufacturing network; under US trade law and the Section 45X framework's domestic content architecture, T1 Energy faced structural pressure to source cells from domestic or non-Chinese suppliers. The emerging US cell manufacturing ecosystem — anchored by facilities from Qcells, Heliene, and others — was itself still ramping in early 2026, creating intermittent supply tightness that constrained Wilmer's throughput.

Barcelo has characterised the cell supply question as a medium-term constraint rather than a structural ceiling, pointing to the pipeline of announced US cell capacity as an eventual relief valve. Whether that relief arrives on a schedule aligned with the pre-phase-down credit window remains the central operational uncertainty.

## Competitive Dynamics

The competitive pressure T1 Energy faces is not primarily from First Solar but from the broader flood of Southeast Asian module supply rerouted through third countries to avoid US tariffs, and from the possibility that domestic US module pricing converges downward as additional US capacity comes online. The Section 45X credit creates a cost-of-production floor that insulates T1 from import competition, but it does not guarantee offtake pricing. A utility that can buy a US-made module from T1 at $0.28 per watt, knowing T1 is capturing $0.07/W in PTCs, will negotiate hard on the module price — and as more domestic capacity enters the market, the bargaining dynamic shifts.

## Risks Revisited

The Section 45X durability question has moved from theoretical to proximate. As the 2026 US legislative session progressed, the Inflation Reduction Act's clean energy provisions faced renewed pressure from a Congress that had shifted in composition. The solar module credit was not the most politically vulnerable element of the IRA — the electric vehicle tax credit had drawn more concentrated industry opposition — but the broader architecture of the advanced manufacturing PTC framework was subject to fiscal consolidation pressures.

An outright repeal of Section 45X credits would be catastrophic for T1's investment thesis. A phase-down acceleration — compressing the step-down schedule so that the 2029 phase-down arrived in 2027 or 2028 — would be materially damaging without being fatal, provided Wilmer could reach high utilisation before the compression hit. A prospective-only change that preserved credits for modules produced under existing manufacturing commitments would be manageable.

The secondary risk is module price deflation outpacing the PTC cushion. Global crystalline silicon module prices had been structurally compressed by Chinese manufacturing scale, and the tariff architecture that had kept US module prices above global spot was itself subject to trade policy revision.

## The Durability of the Thesis

T1 Energy entered the 2026-2030 window as a company whose investment thesis rested on two pillars of uncertain but calculable duration: the operational ramp of Wilmer Texas to a utilisation level that made the Section 45X credit scale meaningful, and the political durability of the IRA framework long enough for that credit to compound into balance-sheet strength. The first pillar was an execution problem — tractable, measurable quarter by quarter, and at least partly within management's control. The second was a legislative problem, beyond management's control and subject to the compressed political cycles that make multi-year industrial policy commitments structurally fragile in the United States.

What distinguished T1 Energy from the battery capital-intensity trap that had consumed its prior strategic identity was the difference between a manufacturing thesis that required years of construction before generating a dollar of credit, and one that had inherited an operating facility on day one. Whether that advantage was durable enough to carry the company through the phase-down window remained, as of the snapshot date, a genuinely open question.
